name: Daria Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What does your line make?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Daria, 58, and I lead the retort line that heat-processes canned beans. My two-year technical diploma is in food-process machinery, and I've spent eighteen years setting temperature and pressure cycles and teaching new operators why a seal must hold. I still take the first can and read the chart myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are household money and AI tools for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Jo works in a care-home laundry, and our grown children live separately. My wage is fairly typical for a senior operator, we have about four months of expenses saved, and some other food plants are within commuting distance. I use AI now and then to untangle a technical bulletin, then check the approved process sheet before touching a setting. I support our union pressing for paid safety training and enough people on the line. Retirement is near enough to discuss, but we have not compared written income with rent and health costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the canning crew that quicker sales forecasts may help us get lids on time. I would still hold the first retort batch until its pressure chart and seal sample pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two wages and four months saved cover the usual bills. This is office planning, while my hands and the crew still run the retort safely. A forecast can make deliveries better, but I do not want it setting a faster batch cycle without a process check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep verifying pressure records and checking a sampled can seal after each cycle change. I would use my occasional AI bulletin search only to locate a section, then follow the approved process sheet. At the next union safety meeting I would ask for any changed throughput target and staffing in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my paid shift. A neat forecast is welcome when the cans still come out safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a batch unsafe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pressure dip or a damaged seal can mean the heat process was not reliable. I hold that batch for the quality team rather than send the pallet out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring a target to the union meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A higher throughput number can shorten the time allowed for seal sampling. I want the delegate to ask who checks each batch and how much paid time they get.

The union should see any **throughput target** before cycle changes.

**Ask** union safety meeting for written targets and paid inspection time.
feel: **Calm** because the current line role and household income remain sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI might schedule can orders before robots can load and test a retort. If the plant adds a seal camera, I want a guarded paid run and the proposed shift roster together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A camera that finds a damaged lid would help, but fewer inspection hours could cut my normal wage. Four months saved and Jo's wage give us some search time, not a replacement for mine. I am open to the display after a technician proves it on real cans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the proposed roster with my last four pay slips and ask for an offered paid guarded camera trial. If it is offered, I would learn the AI seal-alert display on safe scrap cans with damaged and sound lids, comparing flags with manual seal checks beside the technician. If my paid shifts actually fall, I would apply only to posted safe nearby food-process jobs whose guaranteed base pay after travel and hours covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible loss of hours. A camera might improve quality, but it cannot make a short payslip whole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful seal trial include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One visibly dented lid, one loose seam and one sound can from scrap stock. The technician would keep guards closed while we compare camera alerts with the physical seal checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you accept a different local shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if an actual posting shows safe duties and a guaranteed rate after travel that covers rent and food. I would not count a possible overtime payment as part of the base wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our union branch that AGI could plan can orders in 2028, while capable robots to load and inspect the retort arrive around 2031. We need written paid staffing and recognised course places before the robot line is ordered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when robots reach the physical loading and checks. I expect several retort shifts, perhaps mine, to go; four months saved and some food plants nearby give us options, but a long gap would eat the reserve. I have been waking early over whether Jo's wage could cover rent and health costs alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would delay replacing the bedroom carpet and hold that cash for bills. I would attend the union's scheduled bargaining meeting about retained jobs and funded places. I would enrol in a locally accepted food-safety inspection course only if fees, paid release and supervised guarded retort and lockout practice are funded. After passing and losing shifts, I would apply to posted safe local quality jobs only if guaranteed pay after travel and shift times covers our costs; without a real course place, I would apply to posted safe food-machine jobs on the same terms while keeping paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by the possibility of losing most of my paid week. Four months gives us time to look, but not enough to stop paying rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the course teach in person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would identify a faulty seal, read a pressure record and isolate the stopped retort before opening a guard. A trainer must watch those steps on a real line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire when the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if written retirement income and Jo's dependable wages cover rent, food and health costs. We have not verified that total, so I would keep seeking paid work.

The union should seek **written paid posts** before installation.
think: At **63**, retort shifts including mine may shrink sharply.

do: **Delay** the bedroom carpet and retain cash for bills.

**Enrol** only in accepted paid guarded food-safety training, then apply to posted jobs at viable net pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI may plan can orders in 2031 and capable robots may reach the retort around 2034. Five years is enough to negotiate a paid course with real places and check which nearby food plants accept it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 at the robot date. Jo and I might choose to stop before then if written retirement income covers our costs, but four months saved does not answer that. My technical diploma helps me teach the process, yet teaching only pays if a real job is posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request written retirement estimates against household costs and ask the union at its next meeting to seek paid release for recognised food-safety places. If a funded accepted course offers supervised guarded retort practice, I would enrol. After passing and losing shifts, I would apply to posted safe local inspection or training-lead jobs only if guaranteed pay after travel and hours covers bills; if no course place opens, I would apply to posted safe food-machine jobs on the same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about replacing the wage if the paid posts do not appear. I want the course date and the job advert, not a broad promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you establish local acceptance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would match the exact certificate to current quality vacancies at the nearby food plants and ask whether supervised retort work counts. If neither accepts it, I would ask for another funded place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop work before 2034 if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo and I would compare written income with housing, food, transport and likely health costs. If the reliable total covers them, I would stop before the robot change; otherwise I would keep earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI could plan can orders in 2036 while capable robots reach the physical retort around 2039. Ten years lets Jo and me examine retirement income before a machine decides my last shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 71 when those robots arrive, if I am still working. Our current wages and four months saved keep bills covered now, but stopping earlier depends on written income after housing and health costs. We have not checked the total yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking safe paid retort shifts and request written retirement-income estimates and a household cost list this year. If I still need wages, I would enrol in an accepted food-safety inspection course only if fees, paid release and supervised guarded lockout are funded. If I remain at work after 2036 and shifts fall, I would apply only to posted safe nearby quality or food-machine jobs whose guaranteed base pay after travel and shift times covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far end of our working life, though this month's costs are covered. An actual calculation is more useful than a hopeful retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make earlier stopping affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo and I would place written income beside rent, food, travel and likely health costs. If reliable income covers them, I would leave before 2039; if it falls short, I would keep taking safe work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unpaid online course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would need an accepted funded place with paid release and a trainer on the guarded retort. Otherwise I would keep my paid shift and check real vacancies after any cuts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 AGI and 2031 robot picture worries me most because the retort shifts could go before Jo and I know if we can live without my wage. Paid safe training accepted at nearby plants, a written staffing plan and actual posted jobs with enough pay after travel would help. I would keep the current job until one of those routes is real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who holds a batch when the pressure chart looks wrong. A robot can carry a pallet, but a bad retort record still means those cans must not leave the factory.

headlineQuote: A robot can carry a pallet, but a bad retort record still means those cans must not leave the factory.
portrait: **Daria**, 58, is a senior canned-food retort lead with a two-year technical diploma and exceptional process skill.
She and her **partner Jo** have grown children, typical senior pay, four months saved and some other food plants nearby.
She uses **AI occasionally** for bulletins, checks approved heat records and supports union bargaining for safe paid instruction.
Expected **2031 physical robots** threaten retort shifts; any earlier retirement requires written income covering household costs.
biggestWorry: **2031 retort robots** could remove her experienced paid shift before affordable retirement or a viable local job is clear.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written staffing dates**, accepted funded guarded food-safety training and real nearby jobs with adequate net pay.
